extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, MAA members, and academic math community
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians and educators on how the practice and teaching of mathematics should cultivate human flourishing; argues for five central human desires (play, beauty, truth, justice, love) as organizing aims and gives pedagogical and community practices to realize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should make the mind its playground: play is fun, voluntary, has structure and freedom, leads to investigation and surprise, and often carries no great stake in the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach play in class (support inquiry-based and active learning). Play builds hopefulness, community, and perseverance. Teaching play is harder than lecturing because instructors must be ready for many possibilities. Support recreational mathematics and organize activities (competitions, collaborative training) that emphasize community over cutthroat competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics cultivates appreciation of beauty — simplicity, regularity, order, elegance — and pursuing elegant proofs and ideas fosters transcendence and joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivate students through diverse expressions of beauty (art, music, patterns, rigorous arguments, applicability). Encourage search for elegant proofs and emphasize the aesthetic dimensions of mathematics as part of flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (rigorous thinking and intellectual humility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics embodies a quest for truth that trains rigorous thinking, the design of tests/experiments or proofs, and an attitude of intellectual humility (accepting being wrong, celebrating counterexamples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to know when arguments are wrong; reward honest acknowledgment of gaps (e.g., give extra credit on incomplete proofs where students acknowledge gaps). Encourage use of mathematical reasoning in public discourse and value clear, rigorous public writing as scholarly activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice (equity and inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human flourishing in mathematics requires justice: treating others with dignity, recognizing implicit bias, and changing structures and practices that exclude or disadvantage people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have honest conversations about race and marginalization; listen to experiences, be quick to listen and slow to speak. Use documented good practices (see MAA 'Avoiding Implicit Bias') to mitigate bias in selection and evaluation (e.g., take time to make decisions, generate a large candidate pool). Work to change institutional structures and departmental cultures so the community's demographics reflect society; ensure departments do not set up structures that disadvantage students with different backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love (care, advocacy, mentorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Love — caring attention between teacher and student and among colleagues — is essential: being attentive, asking 'What are you going through?', and acting as an advocate for struggling students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a student facing challenges and be a long-term advocate (mentor, pull them toward opportunities, check in when they skip class). Encourage programs like the Math Alliance and personal mentorship to ensure underrepresented students have pathways to graduate study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning / inquiry-based pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Active learning and inquiry-based methods are effective ways to teach the play and investigative aspects of mathematics and improve student learning outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorse and implement active learning practices (CBMS statement referenced). Recognize that active learning requires preparation and flexibility but yields better learning; use classroom designs that allow freedom within structure and student investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating implicit bias in selection and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees and educators should adopt concrete practices to reduce implicit bias that can skew judgments about students and candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MAA's 'Avoiding Implicit Bias' recommendations (examples: take time to make decisions, generate a large candidate pool). Distribute bias-mitigation guidance to committee members and incorporate these practices into hiring, admissions, grading, and awarding processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy and long-term mentorship as a structural practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should act as advocates for students (especially underrepresented/underserved students), providing opportunities, support, and encouragement that can change trajectories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive: present research opportunities, encourage students to study higher math, provide forthright counsel when skills need development but do not prematurely tell students they don't belong. Institutionalize mentorship through programs and personal commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions and tracking should distinguish background from ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Background (prior coursework, placements) is not the same as ability; admissions and tracking policies should avoid using background as a proxy that excludes talented students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit students by demonstrated ability rather than narrow background metrics; provide support after admission. Avoid rigid tracking systems that make students feel they don't belong; reassure and support those with nonstandard trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment practice that rewards honesty and metacognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment design should encourage intellectual humility and honest reflection (e.g., give credit for incomplete proofs when students acknowledge gaps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state exam policies that reward admissions of gaps or partial reasoning to incentivize thoughtful answers over fabricated responses. This yields more thoughtful student work and models how to handle uncertainty and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize community over cutthroat competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitions and collaborative opportunities should emphasize community-building and shared growth rather than only ranking and exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize collaborative training (e.g., inviting teams to train together), celebrate cooperative behavior, and publicly value acts that build community. Use competitions as one way to promote play and perseverance, not as tools to exclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value public writing and broader impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public writing by mathematicians (op-eds, essays) is a form of scholarly activity that communicates rigorous arguments to broader audiences and has measurable broader impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should start valuing public writing in promotion and service decisions. Encourage faculty to shape public understanding of mathematics through writing and outreach; use digital metrics to measure impact when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and name specific intellectual virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics cultivates virtues — hopefulness, perseverance, community, transcendence, joy, rigorous thinking, humility, circumspection — which are important outcomes of teaching and practicing math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula, classroom interactions, and departmental cultures to explicitly cultivate these virtues (e.g., celebrate counterexamples, encourage persistence with problems, model humility). Tell students that you are cultivating humility/rigor as virtues that serve them beyond mathematics.
